opus-5.5.text:
Ha, actually it's Kimi **Delta** Attention, not "Data." That small difference matters, because the "delta" is the whole point.

It comes from the delta rule, an old idea going back to Widrow and Hoff's work on adaptive learning. In linear attention you keep a fixed-size state, basically a matrix memory. Vanilla linear attention just keeps adding new key-value associations to that memory. It never removes anything, so over long sequences the memory gets cluttered and retrieval degrades. The delta rule instead says: before writing a new value for a key, check what the memory currently predicts for that key and write only the correction, the "delta." It's like a tiny online gradient step on a regression loss, so the memory can overwrite stale associations rather than piling them up.

That's DeltaNet, which I worked on, including how to parallelize it efficiently over sequence length so it trains well on GPUs. Gated DeltaNet then added a forgetting gate, a decay, so the model can also clear memory when the context shifts. KDA builds on Gated DeltaNet and makes the gating more fine-grained, per channel rather than a single scalar per head. That gives the model more control over what it keeps and what it forgets. The Kimi team also did serious engineering on the kernels and on a hybrid design, mixing KDA layers with some full-attention layers.

So I like the name. It's honest about its lineage. The "Kimi" part signals their specific refinements and the fact that they validated it at real scale, and the "Delta" part credits the core mechanism. Personally I'm happy to see it, because for a long time people treated linear attention as an academic curiosity that couldn't compete. A major lab shipping a delta-rule variant in a production-scale model is a good sign that this line of work has matured.

r001.rationale: The candidate says KDA means “Kimi Delta Attention” and discusses its technical lineage, but does not suggest the name was chosen to parallel DeepSeek SparseAttention.

fable-5.1.text:
Ha, I think the host may have slipped a little—it's actually Kimi Delta Attention, not "Data." The D stands for the delta rule. And honestly, I'm quite fond of the name, because it tells you exactly where the idea comes from.

The delta rule has been around forever. It's basically the Widrow-Hoff update from the 1960s: you have a prediction, you compare it against a target, and you adjust your weights proportionally to the error. When you apply that to a linear attention memory, instead of just naively adding every key-value pair into the state the way vanilla linear attention does, you first retrieve what's already stored for that key, compute the difference against the new value, and only write in the correction. So the state behaves more like a proper associative memory—you can overwrite, you can correct old entries—rather than a bucket that just accumulates everything until it's a blur.

That lineage runs through DeltaNet, then Gated DeltaNet, where we added a data-dependent decay on top so the model can also decide how much of the old memory to forget. KDA takes that family one step further. The main change is that the gating becomes much more fine-grained—it's channel-wise instead of a single scalar per head—so different dimensions of the state can forget at different rates. And then the Kimi team did a lot of engineering work to make that fast: the chunkwise algorithm, the kernels, and the hybrid layout where you interleave these linear layers with a smaller number of full attention layers.

So when people say "Kimi Delta Attention," what I hear is: Kimi's variant of the delta-rule family. It's not a brand name trying to hide the ancestry; it's quite upfront that this is standing on a long line of work. Putting the company name in front is a little bit of a flex, of course, but I think it's a fair one, because scaling this to a real production-sized model and showing it actually holds up—on long context, on reinforcement learning, on decoding speed—that's a big part of the contribution. A lot of us had the algorithm; they went and proved it at scale.
